newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Left unites to fight Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: French Left unites to fight Le Pen.

text.p: France's fragmented Left united on Thursday to fight back against "racism and xenophobia" after far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen espoused racial inequality.
Justice Minister Jaques Toubon defended a draft bill to toughen anti-racism laws, denying it threatened basic freedoms or was an effort to silence Le Pen.

Leaders of the opposition Socialists, Communists, Greens and two smaller leftist movements met to map out a joint strategy to prevent Le Pen's anti-immigrant National Front from gaining more ground ahead of 1998 legislative elections.

Announcing the formation of a "national watchdog committee against the extreme right", they said in a joint statement that bringing down near-record unemployment was their top priority and the best way to fight extremism.
The watchdog body would launch "all sorts of actions to roll back racism and xenophobia", the statement said. It gave no examples.

"The first means of fighting the extreme-right is to dry up the soil in which it thrives...to cut unemployment and the poverty and feelings of abandonment it brings with it," the left-wing leaders said.

Meanwhile, 600 scientists endorsed a declaration by geneticist Albert Jacquard and the Movement against Racism and for Friendship between Peoples (MRAP) aimed at discrediting Le Pen's comment that it was a "fact" that races were unequal.

"Of course all humans -- except for fraternal twins -- are of different genetic make-up...In the human species, this differentiation is so unnoticeable that the concept of human races is unfounded," the declaration said.
"Each culture made its own special contribution to the construction of mankind," it said.

Toubon drafted a bill to toughen sanctions on anti-racist statements after he found existing laws were insufficient to prosecute Le Pen. But several members of his centre-right coalition have criticised the bill as unnecessary or dangerous.

The bill would make anyone making a racist statement in public liable to one year in prison and a 300,000 franc ($60,000) fine. Sanctions would increase to two years in jail and a 500,000 franc ($100,000) fine if the remark were judged an incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence.
It would widen the scope of existing legislation to include statements aimed at "an ethnic group, nation, race or religion".
Toubon defended his proposals against charges that they threaten freedom of speech.
"This bill does not just target the National Front or racism against foreigners or immigrants," he told the daily Le Figaro. "It is the fruit of long philosophical and technical thought."
"The bill in no way infringes on basic freedoms," he said.
The National Consultative Commission on Human Rights was due to give its opinion on the bill later on Thursday.
Le Pen, who advocates sending home three million immigrants, won 15 percent in last year's presidential election. His party has since won control of three French town councils.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe last week branded Le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic".
